before.approach: From Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20, MP 134) hike the Ross Lake shoreline trail ~7 mi to the Big Beaver Trail junction (or take the Ross Lake Resort water taxi to Big Beaver Landing to shorten this), then continue ~5 mi up Big Beaver Trail to Thirtynine Mile Creek/Camp. Leave the trail there and climb a brushy forested rib to gain the south ridge at a ~6,600 ft saddle. Round trip is roughly 18 miles with 7,000+ ft of elevation gain, typically done over 2-3 days. From the saddle, follow the ridge crest (Class 1-2) past points 7,361 ft and 7,547 ft to a short Class 3 step below the true summit; Luna Camp, about 5 miles farther up Big Beaver Trail, is the start of the separate Southwest Rib route, not this one.

itinerary.cal: North Cascades NP requires a backcountry camping permit for the Pyramid/Colonial basin; best conditions are typically mid-July through September once the Colonial-Neve glacier crossing firms up but before it gets too bare/crevassed.

days.note: From the Pyramid Lake trailhead on Highway 20, climb steadily through forest to Pyramid Lake, then follow the climbers' boot path up the open ridge above it to a campsite around 5,400-5,600 ft, generally the last flat, sheltered ground before the route opens onto glacier terrain. Most parties treat this as a moderate-to-strenuous half-day with full overnight and glacier gear on their backs.
days.title: Approach to ridge camp
days.objective: Reach a ridge camp above Pyramid Lake

days.note: Break camp early, cross the Colonial-Neve glacier basin (rope up; it is crevassed with bergschrunds/moats late season) to the base of Pyramid's southeast slopes, then scramble a loose rock-and-snow finger to the summit ridge. Most parties tag the summit, downclimb to camp, pack up, and continue the full descent to the trailhead the same day, making for a long second day.

before.rope_note: Approach crosses the Colonial Glacier basin (crevasses, steep snow finger) - carry ice axe, crampons, and consider a rope for glacier travel; final ridge/summit is a Class 3 rock scramble, typically unroped.

pitch_detail.notes: Roughly 10 minutes along the highway before leaving it just east of Happy Creek.
pitch_detail.pitch: Highway/closure gate to Happy Creek Nature Trail split

pitch_detail.notes: Follows the well-built nature trail up the east side of Happy Creek to a cascading waterfall.
pitch_detail.pitch: Happy Creek Nature Trail to waterfall (~1.5 mi)

pitch_detail.notes: Path steepens and grows fainter but stays followable; crosses a boulder field that is hazardous without snow cover.
Snow cover typically begins near 2,800 ft; continue up the north-side terrain to the summit.

itinerary.cal: Same FR-1570 washout access as the standard route; crampons/axe are typically still needed on the ridge's upper snow slopes even in summer.

days.note: Same brushy FR-1570/Kindy Ridge approach as the standard route to a camp near Cyclone Lake; some parties instead push higher to a bivy at 6,300 ft on the ridge itself to shorten summit day.
days.title: Approach to Cyclone Lake camp
days.objective: Reach camp near Cyclone Lake (~4,800 ft)

days.note: From camp, cross heather and easy slabs onto Snowking's East Ridge, staying off the glacier to the right; the final few hundred feet steepens to about 30 degrees below the summit block (easy 3rd class). Round trip to the summit runs about 2 hours per multiple trip reports; the team then breaks camp and hikes all the way out.
days.title: East Ridge summit push and hike-out

schedule.label: Leave Cyclone Lake camp
schedule.detail: Crampons/axe on for the ridge's snow sections.

schedule.label: Summit (7,433 ft)
schedule.detail: Via the East Ridge, Class 2-3 near the top.

days.objective: Climb the East Ridge to the 7,433 ft summit, then hike out

itinerary.totalNote: A 2-day trip is standard: ~6 mi and ~4,700 ft to a Cyclone Lake camp on day 1, then a fast, non-technical East Ridge summit push (~2 hrs, ~2,000-2,600 ft per real trip reports) plus the full hike-out on day 2; very fit parties have done the whole thing car-to-car in about 9 hours, but most treat it as an overnight.

before.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass (or $8 day-use fee) recommended for parking at the Cascade River Road/FR-1570 trailhead.
access.notes: No reservation, lottery, or quota system applies to this Glacier Peak Wilderness approach; access is via the free self-issued trailhead permit noted under "permit."
access.rules: Standard Wilderness Act group-size limit (12) applies; no bear-canister requirement or NPS-style off-trail cross-country zone cap is documented for this Forest Service approach.
access.permit: No climbing permit required, but a free self-issued wilderness travel permit must be filled out at the trailhead register when entering the Glacier Peak Wilderness. Overnight camping along the route (Cyclone Lake basin, ridge bivies) is dispersed/undesignated.
access.closures: FR-1570 has a long-standing washout near the Cascade River crossing that keeps vehicles from reaching the historical trailhead; verify current road status with the Mt. Baker Ranger District before driving in.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mt. Baker Ranger District (Sedro-Woolley office, 810 State Route 20, Sedro-Woolley, WA 98284)
access.land_manager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — Glacier Peak Wilderness (Mt. Baker Ranger District)
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / America the Beautiful Pass

overnight_permit.where: Sign the wilderness register at the trailhead where one exists.

weather.typical: Typical North Cascades alpine summer weather within the best-season window; consistent with the existing climate/access data for this remote, glaciated peak
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are a known hazard on this route, most common in July-August

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Moderate - Class 2-3 terrain is not steep/technical, but the long, committing approach and the crevassed glacier crossing mean the main consequence of a mistake is a remote rescue scenario rather than a rock-fall-exposure scenario

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer route (climbed in the Jul-Sep snow-free/glacier-travel window, outside NWAC's Nov-Apr winter forecast season; nearest NWAC coverage for this area is the West Slopes North zone)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Real hazard, not N/A - the existing hazards list names crevasse fall on the Snowking Glacier specifically; the glacier is best traveled once well-covered (mid-summer) and roped travel is warranted even where snow appears to bridge crevasses

itinerary.cal: FR-1570 (Kindy Creek Rd) has a washout, so parking is below the road-end, adding mileage; best done June-September when the Snowking Glacier has consolidated snow and the approach trail is mostly clear.

days.note: From the FR-1570 washout parking, follow the old logging road and then the boot-beaten Kindy Ridge climbers' trail up through brush and subalpine terrain, topping out around Point 5,791 before dropping to camp near Cyclone Lake. Expect a rough, steep, brushy trail with little flat ground.
days.title: Approach to Cyclone Lake camp
days.objective: Reach camp in the meadows near Cyclone Lake (~4,800 ft)

days.note: An alpine start gets the rope team onto the Snowking Glacier while the snow is firm; climbers rope up for crevasse hazard on the ascent. After summiting, the team downclimbs to camp, breaks it down, and continues the long hike out the same day — though many parties instead camp a second night and hike out on a third day.

schedule.label: Back at camp, break down tents

schedule.detail: Long day if hiking all the way out.

days.objective: "Climb the Snowking Glacier to the 7,433 ft summit, then descend all the way to the car"

itinerary.totalNote: A 2-day overnight trip is the standard: ~6.5 mi and ~4,700 ft to a Cyclone Lake camp on day 1, then a roped glacier summit push plus the full hike-out (~8.5 mi, ~2,700 ft gain / ~6,200 ft loss) on day 2; some parties split the hike-out into a third day.

pro_tips: Go early-to-mid summer for the most continuous, safest glacier travel — by August the glacier opens up and crevasse hazard rises noticeably.
Camp at Cyclone Lake (~4,800 ft) to split the trip into two easier days in one of the nicer basins in the area.
Budget extra time versus older trip reports — the FR-1570 washout means most parties now gain more elevation than historical route descriptions assume.
A drier, non-glacier alternative approaches via the West Ridge from Illabot Creek — used by some parties in late season once the Snowking Glacier route is mostly bare and awkward.
